newsitem.title: MALI: RTRS - Mali not impressed with sale of BHP division.
newsitem.headline: RTRS - Mali not impressed with sale of BHP division.

text.p: Mali's government is unlikely to hinder Randgold Resources' purchase of BHP Minerals Mali, but it is unhappy about the way the deal proceeded, a senior government official said.
The sale would give Randgold a controlling stake in Syama goldmine, one of West Africa's biggest.
"On the side of the government there should be no particular obstacle to this sale," the official told Reuters.
He said one of the main criteria -- the credibility of the new partner -- was not in doubt because Randgold was one of South Africa's biggest mining houses.
But he said the sale may not have followed the procedure set out in a convention signed by BHP and the government.
"The terms of the sales contract could be at odds with this convention which stipulates precise conditions for exploitation, production and employment," he said.
The sale agreement had not been submitted to the government yet, he added.
Senior officials in the Finance and Mines ministries bemoaned the lack of communication between the two companies and the government.
"Everything seemed to pass between the companies as if they were relegating the government to a mere onlooker," one said.

Randgold Resources, the exploration and new business arm of Randgold and Exploration Co Ltd, said on September 3 that it had taken control of BHP Minerals Mali from Australia's Broken Hill Proprietary Co Ltd (BHP).

It said the deal, including a 65 percent stake in the Syama mine and BHP's exploration interests in Mali, was worth $30 million cash, a $23 million loan claim and a $31 million loan to be retained by BHP and paid back over six years.
Mali's government has a 20 percent stake in SOMISY, Syama's operating company, and the International Finance Corp holds 15 percent.

Randgold Resource's chief executive Mark Bristow told Reuters that it aimed to raise Syama's gold output to 200,000 ounces a year from 125,000 ounces by bringing in new machining methods and boosting staff morale.
He did not say when he expected the target to be reached.
Syama's estimated resources amount to 110 tonnes of gold at an in situ grade of 4.1 grammes/tonne.
BHP put its stake on the market after problems with mining deeper ores, the introduction of import duties on equipment by Mali and staff stoppages.

The general manager of BHP Minerals Mali, Alan Miskirin, told Reuters that the firm's partnership with the government, the first Mali had signed with a multinational company, had been an "apprenticeship" for both parties.

"We have been victims of several criticisms, tied in my view to a lack of communication. In Africa, people think of mines as money, and nothing but money, but forget the work that has to go in beforehand to get this gold and this money," he said.
BHP said the sale of BHP Minerals Mali Inc to Randgold Resources was at A$45 million ($36 million) below book value and this would be reflected in its August quarter results.
